description: The AVMK Frontier Labs team consists of 3 high school kids and 1 middle schooler from Houston, Texas. Our members are, Abyaz, Victor, Keerti, and Marvin. We are interested in space exploration, technology, coding, and exploring new ideas. We can turn creative concepts into real world solutions. We are excited to participate in this NASA hackathon to push our skills beyond the classroom, and build something that makes a difference.
summary:
Frontier Labs is a free, browser-based platform that quantifies how closely any Earth analog site matches candidate permanent Moon base locations or Mars exploration zones, using real NASA data, not reputation.
Mission planners have long relied on well-known sites like the Atacama Desert and Haughton Crater for astronaut training and equipment testing, but no one had ever measured the actual similarity across multiple scientific dimensions. We built a multi-criteria scoring engine applying four original mathematical similarity functions — Gaussian, logarithmic ratio, Jaccard set similarity, and boolean agreement — to open NASA datasets covering topography, surface temperature, and mineralogy. Every result returns a Similarity Index (0–100%) with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval and a component breakdown explaining what matches, what doesn't, and by exactly how much.
Validated against Shackleton Crater (the leading Artemis permanent base candidate), the tool identified Haughton Crater as the strongest lunar south-pole analog, with a composite similarity of 36–48%. It also surfaces previously underused sites — Duvanny Yar (Russia, 63–80% for Martian ice zones) and Bockfjorden (Svalbard) — that standard analog lists miss entirely.
The tool requires no installation, runs offline after first load, supports 15 languages including Arabic RTL, and offers six audience modes from K–8 students to mission planners — making rigorous planetary analog science accessible to everyone.
details:
Presentation Slides:

https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wU85XlKQhFgnAv_fYvaKeR7GOuGckpbkdRBVuMhqjM4/edit?usp=sharing

What It Does

Frontier Labs is an interactive analog scoring tool that lets any user — from a student to an aerospace engineer — select a planetary target on the Moon or Mars, choose an Earth candidate site, set mission-profile weight sliders (General Survey, Permanent Base, Landing Site, or Rover Mobility), load curated NASA data from the built-in library, and receive a quantified Similarity Index with full scientific transparency.

The tool currently compares six Earth analog sites (Atacama Desert, Mauna Kea Hawaii, Haughton Crater Devon Island, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Askja Iceland, Rio Tinto Spain) against lunar south-pole targets (including Shackleton, Mons Mouton, Haworth, and de Gerlache) and Martian mid-latitude zones (Arcadia Planitia, Jezero Crater, Utopia Planitia, Deuteronilus Mensae, Phlegra Montes). It evaluates three dimensions by default — temperature, topography, and surface composition — with expansion to additional factors planned on the roadmap.

How It Works

Stage 1 — Data Ingestion: The platform fuses open multi-agency datasets covering lunar topography (NASA LRO LOLA, 240 m polar DEM), lunar thermal context (LRO Diviner), Mars elevation (MOLA–HRSC blended DEM, 200 m), Earth surface temperature (NASA Terra/Aqua MODIS MOD11A2 v061), Earth terrain (NASADEM and ESA Copernicus GLO-30), and geology/soil (Macrostrat API, ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0, ESA Permafrost CCI v5.0).

Stage 2 — AVMK Similarity Engine: Four mathematical functions normalize each feature comparison into a score in [0, 1]:

  • Gaussian Similarity for continuous metrics (slope σ=5°, mean surface temperature σ=35 K)
  • Logarithmic Ratio Similarity for scale-spanning metrics (local relief, thermal amplitude, aridity)
  • Jaccard Similarity for surface lithology, comparing mineral/rock tag sets: |A∩B| / |A∪B|
  • Boolean Agreement for binary features (impact craters, lava tubes, ground ice presence)

The weighted composite Similarity Index is computed only over criteria with valid measurements on both sides: Similarity Index = 100 × [Σ(wᵢ × sᵢ) / Σwᵢ]. Missing data is excluded — never imputed as zero — and results with less than 60% weight coverage are automatically flagged as low confidence.

Stage 3 — Results & Transparency: Each output returns a Similarity Index, 95% bootstrap confidence interval, component-level breakdown bars, a verdict label (Strong ≥60% / Moderate 40–59% / Limited <40%), and a "Why Not Others?" diagnostic explaining why lower-ranked sites were excluded. An Honest Limitations Panel explicitly notes that no Earth site can replicate lunar gravity (0.16g), Mars gravity (0.38g), hard vacuum or thin CO₂ atmosphere, cosmic radiation flux, or electrostatic regolith dust — which the challenge specifically requires teams to acknowledge.

Stage 4 — Platform Architecture: The tool runs entirely client-side on GitHub Pages with zero backend dependency, achieving sub-second response times. It includes a Marvin-AI assistant (helper.js), 15 languages with RTL Arabic support, six audience modes (Explorer K–8 through Scientist and Mission Planner), 30 NASA data files, 21 premade comparison sets, an image interpreter mode, a Python package (analog_engine.py with the same math as the JavaScript, plus accuracy_check.py with 27 validation checks), and an offline built-in mode with cached templates.

Key Results

  • Shackleton Crater (Moon) — validation case: Haughton Crater, Canada: 36–48% composite (impact breccia + buried ice stability + cold hyper-arid). Beacon Valley, Antarctica: 32–44% (sublimation ice + permafrost). Nain Plutonic Suite: strongest anorthositic mineralogical match.
  • Jezero Crater (Mars) — temperature run: Haughton Crater, Devon Island: 27% (Bootstrap 95% CI: 25–28%). Daytime overlap 66%, night-time overlap 0%, day-night swing 5%. Verdict: Limited analog.
  • Martian mid-latitude ice zones: Duvanny Yar, Russia: 63–80% (ice-rich permafrost + cold volcanic terrain — a site most analog lists miss entirely).
  • Control case: Atacama Desert vs. Gale Crater: 31% — driven by a 38°C daytime temperature gap. Reputation ≠ data.

Why It's Creative & Different

Most analog comparisons produce a list. Frontier Labs produces a score, a confidence range, a component breakdown, and an explanation of failure modes — all from the same open NASA data sources judges can verify. The tool surfaces analytically strong but underused sites (Duvanny Yar, Bockfjorden, Tso Kar in Ladakh) that standard literature overlooks, fulfilling the challenge's specific call to "look beyond well-known analog sites." The platform is not a report — it is a reusable, reproducible decision-support tool any team can run on any comparison they choose.

Tools, Languages & Technologies

  • Languages: JavaScript (client-side scoring engine), Python (analog_engine.py, accuracy_check.py)
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages (zero-cost, zero-backend, offline-capable)
  • Data formats supported: CSV, TSV, JSON, PNG elevation/temperature maps
  • AI assistant: Marvin-AI (helper.js, integrated Claude-compatible interface)
  • Localization: 15 languages, RTL Arabic, 6 audience modes
  • Data sources: NASA LRO LOLA, LRO Diviner, MOLA–HRSC, Terra/Aqua MODIS, NASADEM, ESA Copernicus GLO-30, Macrostrat API, ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0, ESA Permafrost CCI v5.0, NASA PDS, GIBS, POWER
